summary: A major working temple in Chiang Mai’s western Old City, best visited for its Lanna architecture and layered complex rather than as a quick exterior photo stop. The Tourism Authority of Thailand identifies Wihan Lai Kham, the main viharn, the scripture library and mural paintings among its highlights.
whyGo: See several important Lanna buildings and decorative traditions in one central temple compound.
Visit a living religious site associated with the revered Phra Buddha Sihing image.
Fit a thoughtful temple stop into an Old City walking day.
bestFor: First-time Chiang Mai visitors interested in heritage and architecture
Travellers exploring the western Old City on foot
Visitors who can take time to look beyond the main hall
skipIf: You have already visited several similar temple complexes and want a different activity.
You need confirmed step-free access throughout the site.
You expect a quiet, uncrowded atmosphere at any time of day.
duration: Planning estimate: 45–90 minutes for the main compound; allow longer if you want to examine the buildings and murals carefully.
cost: The current TAT listing does not state an admission charge. Budget for possible donations or separately ticketed areas, but confirm at the entrance; no fee was verified.
hours: TAT lists daily opening from 06:00 to 18:00. Confirm locally before a time-sensitive visit, as worship or temple operations can affect access to individual buildings.
bestTime: Go early for a calmer visit and softer light. Midday is hotter and busier; this is a planning suggestion rather than a published crowd forecast.
gettingThere: The temple is on Sam Lan Road in the Phra Singh area of the Old City. Walk from nearby Old City accommodation; from farther away, use a songthaew, tuk-tuk or ride-hailing car and specify Wat Phra Singh Woramahawihan. No current route or fare information was verified.
booking: No advance booking is indicated by TAT for an ordinary visit. Ask at the entrance about access to individual halls and any current fee or donation guidance.
accessibility: The official TAT listing notes parking and toilets but does not describe step-free routes, accessible toilets or wheelchair access. Expect a historic temple setting and confirm specific access needs directly before travelling.
practicalTips: Cover shoulders and knees; remove shoes where signs or worship practice require it.
Keep voices low, give worshippers room and ask before photographing people.
Carry small cash in case donations or a fee are requested.
Check which buildings are open when you arrive; access may differ within the compound.
decemberNotes: December is generally a popular, relatively cooler travel period in Chiang Mai, so allow a little extra time if the Old City is busy. This is seasonal planning guidance, not a December 2026 forecast. No special December 2026 event or closure was verified.
uncertainties: TAT gives hours and contact numbers but does not publish an admission price or detailed accessibility information.
Opening of individual halls, current visitor rules and December 2026 exceptions were not independently confirmed.
Transport fares and drop-off conditions vary; check with the driver before setting out.
